quotes.text: Hänsel und Gretel blends Wagnerian orchestration with accessible melodies and has endured as a perennial favorite in opera repertoires worldwide.

In Naples, he encountered Richard Wagner, whose invitation led to Humperdinck's assistance on the 1882 premiere of Parsifal in Bayreuth and tutoring of Wagner's son Siegfried, cementing his alignment with Wagnerian techniques of leitmotif and rich harmony evident in his mature works.

Humperdinck composed Hänsel und Gretel as incidental music for his sister's puppet play, expanding it into a full opera premiered on 23 December 1893 at the Hoftheater in Weimar under Richard Strauss's baton, achieving immediate acclaim for its enchanting score and family-friendly narrative.
Die Königskinder (1910), which pioneered Sprechgesang—a half-spoken vocal style later adopted by Schoenberg—marked Humperdinck as a bridge between Wagnerian grandeur and emerging modernism.

From 1880 to 1881, Humperdinck participated directly in the Bayreuth Festival, assisting with the rehearsal and premiere of Wagner's Parsifal. This role allowed him to observe and contribute to Wagner's use of leitmotifs, expansive orchestration, and integrated vocal-instrumental textures firsthand, while also serving as music tutor to Wagner's son Siegfried. These experiences solidified Wagner's dominance as Humperdinck's primary influence, emphasizing continuous musical development over discrete numbers and fostering a commitment to mythological and symbolic narrative structures in opera.

Around 1882, Humperdinck resided briefly in Paris after securing the Meyerbeer Prize, encountering the lighter, more melodic French operatic style exemplified by composers like Charles Gounod and Ambroise Thomas. However, this exposure reinforced rather than supplanted his preference for the denser, psychologically intensive German Romantic tradition derived from Wagner, as evidenced by his subsequent works' adherence to through-composed forms and chromatic harmony over French opéra comique conventions.

"Funny How Time Slips Away" penned by Willie Nelson and recorded a multitude of times over the last six decades swirls Engelbert's rich vocal, a classic orchestral arrangement, and a bit of country all together and gives Humperdinck another quiver in his arsenal or great songs to pull from when performing.
"Let It Be Me" is another track that pushes the 60 year-old-mark and sees Humperdinck putting a classicly modern spin on the track.
The ebb and flow in Engelbert's voice demonstrates his ability to convey his emotion without over doing it.

The arrangement lends itself to Engelbert's voice and allows him to show flashes of both his upper and lower registers. Listening to this version, it gives you a glimpse into the classic feel and treatment Humperdinck wanted to deliver keeping the original intact while putting his own spin on it.
Humperdinck's treatment of disc closer "Blue Christmas" is a class and country crossover that should please his fans all over the world.

A decade later, his sister, Adelheid Wette, asked for some folksongs to accompany her rendition of Hänsel und Gretel (1893), which eventually morphed into a fully staged opera.

The composer stayed with the fairy tale genre for his next few staged works: Die sieben Geislein (The Seven Little Children, 1895), based on another Grimm fantasy; Dornröschen (Sleeping Beauty, 1902); and Königskinder (The King's Children, 1897), a didactic allegorical melodrama by Ernst Rosmer that exploited the Wagnerian theory of Sprechgesang.

The latter work was commissioned by the venerable stage director Max Reinhardt, who had previously engaged Humperdinck to compose incidental music for four Shakespeare plays: The Merchant of Venice, The Winter's Tale, The Tempest and Twelfth Night.
